:::{.callout-learning}
After completing this session, you will be able to:

- Explain why reading data from URLs is more reproducible than using hardcoded local file paths
- Apply a file-existence cache pattern to avoid redundant downloads in R scripts
- Use `read_waterdata_monitoring_location()` and `read_waterdata_combined_meta()` to discover USGS monitoring stations and available data
- Retrieve daily water data for monitoring stations using `read_waterdata_daily()`
- Visualize water temperature time series and seasonal patterns with `ggplot2`
- Describe the client-server model and explain how HTTP APIs work conceptually
- Construct a basic API request using `httr2` *(optional)*
:::

## Overview

One of the most common reproducibility barriers in data-driven science isn't in the analysis
code itself, but rather in how data gets loaded in the first place. A script full of hardcoded file
paths like `read_csv("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/data_final_v3.csv")` might work perfectly on one
machine and fail immediately on every other.

Getting data **programmatically** -- directly in your code, from a remote source -- solves this
problem. In this session, we'll move from ad-hoc data downloads to systematic, reproducible data
access. We'll learn a caching pattern for downloading files reliably, then use the `dataRetrieval`
package to retrieve and visualize USGS streamflow data from monitoring stations. Along the
way, we'll peek under the hood at how web APIs work.
